newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rand option volatilities at 14-month low.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rand option volatilities at 14-month low.

text.p: Implied volatility options on the South African rand have fallen to their lowest levels since February 1996 following the currency's new-found stability.
On Friday, dealers said one-month volatilies on the currency were trading at between 4.5 and 5.5 percent.
"That is down from around 30 percent in its heyday in February last year when things were wild," an options trader said, adding that volatilities had also fallen across the one-year year area.
A speculative attack on the rand, which began on February 16 last year, knocked it from around 3.65 against the dollar to an all-time low of 4.7670 bid by end-October.
This year, the rand has firmed from around 4.70 and has traded between 4.40 and 4.50 since early February.
"The volatilities have been coming back all the time, indicating that the rand is quite stable and the market thinks it is going to continue that way for quite some time," an options trader said.

"The rand has done very little for an extended period of time now and the implied volatilities are simply moving back to the actual experience volatility in the underlying spot," another options trader said.
Traders noted that while London players had been large sellers of options on Thursday, the move lower came on the back of generally thin volumes.
"The market is a mixture of local and offshore banks ...but it has been thin. Its a question of a little bit of selling coming from various sources," a trader said.
The rand has benefited this year from investment flows into South Africa's bond and equity markets.
The bond market has notched up net foreign purchases of more than nine billion rand so far this year, while the foreigners have also been net buyers of almost five billion rand's worth of equities.
That has made the Reserve Bank's job of maintaining stability in the foreign exchange market much easier.
"As opposed to leaning against the wind last year, the Reserve Bank is not having a problem. The winds are very favourable at the moment," a trader said.
Dealers said the rand was expected to benefit further in months ahead from large export orders as well as inflows of proceeds from government's privatisation programme.
Some $1.26 billion is expected to flow into the market over the next month or so from the government's sale of a 30 percent stake in telecommunications utility Telkom to U.S. and Malaysian operators.
Dealers said there remained pressure for implied volatilities to fall further, indicating an extended period of stability for the rand
"Fair value on the rand at the moment is about 4.35 on a purchasing power parity (PPP) basis between now and the end of the year," one trader said.
"That indicates that the rand is going to be relatively stable until PPP catches up with 4.45, which will only be next year," he said.
